ALL.text:
Allstate's rank is built on two pillars: Growth at 95.5 and Value at 90.6. The growth figure comes almost entirely from a reported 101.7% year-over-year revenue increase, which is an unusually large jump for a mature property-casualty insurer with a $69B market cap. For insurers, the top line blends premiums earned with investment results, so a doubling often reflects a swing from prior-year investment losses to gains, or a base-period distortion, rather than a doubling of policies in force. That is worth checking in the underlying statements before treating the growth score at face value. The value side is more straightforward: a 6.71 P/E, 6.98 P/FCF and 1.02 P/S are cheap on an absolute basis, though the 2.25x price-to-book is not especially low for the sector, which is a hint that the cheapness sits in earnings rather than in assets.

Quality scores a middling 59.1 despite a 33.6% ROE, largely because several inputs — ROIC, operating and gross margins, Piotroski, Altman — are unavailable for this filer, so the score leans on a thin evidence base. Leverage looks conservative at 0.24 debt-to-equity. Momentum at 69.9 is solid but not extreme, so the stock is not obviously stretched after a run.

The main thing the numbers may be hiding is cyclicality. A 15.2% net margin and 33.6% ROE are strong for a P&C underwriter and typically appear late in a hard pricing cycle, after rate increases have outrun claims inflation. A single-digit P/E on peak-cycle earnings can look expensive if loss ratios normalize or catastrophe seasons turn severe. Reserve development and auto/home rate adequacy are the specifics to verify.

GOOG.text:
Alphabet's #32 ranking and 56.7 final score are built on three fairly strong factors — Growth (72.3), Quality (66.5) and Momentum (66.4) — dragged down by a weak Value score (22.7). The Growth reading is supported by 15.1% year-over-year revenue growth and a punchier 34.2% EPS growth, suggesting margin expansion and share buybacks are amplifying bottom-line gains beyond top-line pace. Quality is anchored by genuinely elite profitability: 31.8% ROE, 27.7% ROIC, a 59.7% gross margin and roughly 32% operating and net margins. The balance sheet reinforces this — Debt/Equity of just 0.12, a 2.01 current ratio, and an extraordinarily high Altman Z-Score of 16.28 point to minimal financial-distress risk. Momentum in the mid-60s indicates the stock has been performing well relative to peers.

The obvious tension is valuation. A P/E of 31.6, P/B of 10.05, P/S of 10.36 and especially P/FCF near 57 explain the depressed 22.7 Value score — buyers are paying a premium, and the model flags little margin of safety. Worth double-checking: FCF growth was essentially flat at 0.69%, a sharp divergence from the 34% EPS growth, which may reflect heavy capital expenditure (likely AI/data-center spending) consuming cash. The Piotroski F-Score of 6/9 is solid but not pristine, hinting at some softness beneath the headline profitability. Finally, with Momentum already elevated, readers should consider how much good news is already reflected in the price, and whether the stretched P/FCF leaves room for disappointment.

ANET.text:
Arista Networks lands at #29 on the strength of three of its four factors. Momentum (77) and Growth (76.3) are the primary engines: revenue climbed 28.6% year-over-year, EPS 22.95%, and free cash flow 15.67%, confirming the business is still expanding at a healthy clip. Quality (68.6) is also solid, supported by a 28.39% ROE, a 64.06% gross margin, and an exceptional 42.82% operating margin and 38.99% net margin — this is a highly profitable operation. The balance sheet looks pristine, with a 3.05 current ratio and an Altman Z-Score of 22.54 that signals essentially no bankruptcy risk. What drags the composite down to 56.8 is Value, scoring just 6.8, near the bottom of the universe.

That Value score is the number a reader should sit with. At a P/E of 67.41, P/S of 26.28, P/B of 19.13, and P/FCF of 55.66, the market has priced in years of continued rapid growth; any deceleration in the growth or momentum figures could weigh heavily given how little valuation cushion exists. The Piotroski F-Score of 5/9 is only middling despite the strong headline profitability, worth checking against the specific components (asset turnover, share issuance, margin trend). Also note momentum this strong often reflects a stock late in a run, and ROIC and leverage metrics are listed as "n/a," so verify capital efficiency and any off-balance-sheet obligations directly from filings rather than relying on the model's gaps.

CFG.text:
Citizens Financial's #22 ranking and 57.5 composite are built primarily on its Value and Momentum scores, with Growth playing a supporting role and Quality acting as the clear drag. On valuation, the stock screens cheaply for a regional bank: a P/E near 16.6, a P/B of just 1.16, and a P/FCF around 13.8 all place it in the upper tier (72.6) of the ranked universe. Momentum at 67.6 suggests the shares have participated in a broader recovery, and Growth of 55.2 is underpinned by 26.2% EPS growth, 10.5% FCF growth, and roughly 5.6% revenue growth year over year. The standout signal is a perfect Piotroski F-Score of 9/9, which points to broad-based improvement across profitability, leverage, and operating efficiency. Net margin of 22.2% and modest leverage (debt/equity 0.43) round out a reasonably clean picture.

The weak link is Quality at 38, and the reason sits in plain sight: ROE of just 6.96% is low for a bank, meaning profitability on the equity base is thin despite the healthy F-Score. A reader should weigh whether the cheap P/B reflects genuine value or simply the market pricing in that subpar return on equity. It is also worth checking whether the strong 26% EPS growth is a durable trend or a rebound off a depressed base, and how sensitive Citizens' net interest margin and credit provisions are to the rate environment, since many banking metrics here (ROIC, coverage ratios) are unavailable for cross-checking.

LLY.text:
Eli Lilly lands at #16 with a 60.4 score built almost entirely on the growth and momentum side of the model. Growth scores an exceptional 92.9, backed by 44.7% year-over-year revenue growth, 95.6% EPS growth and 90.7% FCF growth — figures that reflect the ongoing surge in demand for its diabetes and weight-loss franchise. Momentum adds 81, indicating the stock has been among the stronger performers in the universe. Quality is respectable at 67.4, supported by an elite 83% gross margin, 31.7% net margin, a 77.8% ROE and a near-perfect Piotroski F-Score of 8/9, which signals broadly improving fundamentals across profitability, leverage and efficiency.

The glaring weak spot is Value at just 5.2 — effectively the bottom of the ranked universe. A P/E of 54, P/B of 42, P/S of 17 and P/FCF of 67 mean investors are paying steep multiples that price in continued rapid expansion; any deceleration in growth could weigh heavily given how much optimism is embedded.

Readers should note a few things the headline numbers may obscure. The 81 momentum score comes after a strong run, so the stock may be extended. The very high ROE is flattered by leverage — debt/equity sits at 1.6 — and several fields (ROIC, operating margin, Altman Z) are marked n/a, limiting a full quality picture. The core question is whether the extraordinary growth rates can persist enough to justify a valuation the model ranks near dead last.

ADI.text:
Analog Devices lands at #16 with a final score of 53.4, and the ranking is clearly powered by its Momentum (83.6) and Growth (77.9) factors. The growth story is concrete: revenue is up 29.75% year-over-year, EPS has jumped 83.19%, and free cash flow grew 37%, with a recent 5.33% earnings surprise reinforcing the upward trend. The business itself shows genuine quality in its margin structure — a 64.49% gross margin, 32.5% operating margin, and 26.01% net margin are strong for a semiconductor company — and a Piotroski F-Score of 8/9 signals healthy fundamental momentum. Leverage is modest, with debt/equity at 0.26 and a current ratio of 1.75.

The tension lies in the two weaker factors. Value scores just 19.3, and the multiples explain why: a P/E of 58, P/S of 15.13, P/B of 5.74, and P/FCF of 42 all price ADI as an expensive stock. Quality is only middling at 40.3 despite those fat margins, because returns on capital are thin — ROE of 9.79% and ROIC of 7.79% are unremarkable, and gross profit/assets of 14.1% suggests a heavy, capital-intensive balance sheet.

A reader should weigh a few things. The eye-catching EPS and revenue growth likely reflect recovery off a cyclical trough, so those rates may not be sustainable — semiconductor demand is notoriously cyclical. High momentum can also arrive late in a run. And a rich valuation leaves little cushion if growth decelerates or ROIC stays subdued relative to the price being paid.

TER.text:
Teradyne's #9 ranking is overwhelmingly a momentum story, with a near-top-decile momentum score of 96.7 doing most of the heavy lifting. That's backed by real fundamental strength: revenue grew 30.3% year-over-year, EPS jumped 52.9%, and the latest earnings surprise of 20.5% suggests the business is beating expectations as the semiconductor test cycle turns. Quality is solid at 59.3, supported by a 29.7% ROE, 28.7% ROIC, and healthy margins (58.7% gross, 26.5% operating). The balance sheet is pristine — essentially zero debt, a 2.15 current ratio, and an Altman Z-Score of 26.1 that signals virtually no bankruptcy risk. Growth at 66.8 rounds out a picture of a profitable, expanding, financially sound company.

The glaring weakness is Value, scoring just 4.7 — near the bottom of the universe. Investors are paying a steep price for that growth and momentum: a P/E of 65.9, P/B of 13.76, P/S of 14.87, and a P/FCF above 100. Those multiples leave little margin for error if growth decelerates.

A reader should double-check a few tensions. First, the momentum score is very high, which often comes late in a run and can reverse sharply in cyclical semiconductor names. Second, despite strong EPS growth, free cash flow actually fell 5%, and the Piotroski F-Score of 6/9 is only moderate — worth reconciling against the rosy income-statement figures. Finally, the rich valuation means much of the good news may already be priced in.

PNC.text:
PNC's #17 ranking and 53.4 composite are anchored by its Value factor (73.4), the standout among its four scores. On the surface the valuation is undemanding: a P/E of 14.0, P/B of 1.31, and P/FCF of 14.8 are modest for a large-cap bank, and a 28.83% net margin alongside a 34.54% operating margin reflects the typically high-margin economics of a diversified financial institution. Growth (55.2) and Momentum (51.1) both sit near the middle of the pack, so the stock is neither leading nor lagging on price trend, while reported revenue growth of 72.27% is eye-catching and helps the Growth reading.

The clear drag is Quality at 37.6, the weakest factor and a meaningful counterweight given Quality carries the largest weight in the model. ROE of 11.98% and ROIC of just 6.89% are unremarkable, and the Debt/Equity of 0.71 reflects the leverage inherent to a bank's balance sheet — worth noting that many quality sub-metrics (Altman Z, Piotroski, current ratio, gross margin) read "n/a," which is normal for financials but means the Quality score rests on a thinner set of inputs.

A reader should scrutinize the growth figures: 72.27% revenue growth is unusually large and likely reflects accounting or comparison-base quirks common in bank revenue, not sustainable organic expansion. It also sits against a -44.4% decline in free cash flow, a divergence worth understanding. The near-flat 0.84% earnings surprise suggests results are landing broadly in line with expectations rather than accelerating.

PFG.text:
Principal Financial Group's #13 ranking (54.8/100) is anchored by its Value score of 81.6, comfortably its strongest factor. The valuation metrics support this: a P/E of 15.52, P/B of 1.65, P/S of 1.57 and an especially cheap-looking P/FCF of 6.68 all point to a stock that is not richly priced relative to its earnings and cash generation. Momentum at 65.1 is respectable, suggesting price action has been supportive, and the modest 2.26% earnings surprise indicates the business is roughly meeting expectations. Working against these are Quality (35) and Growth (38.2), both below the midpoint. ROE of 13.35% and ROIC of 9.98% are decent but not standout for a financial, and the Piotroski F-Score of 6/9 is middling. Leverage is conservative, with Debt/Equity at 0.33.

A reader should weigh what the value score may be masking. Revenue growth is slightly negative (-1.76%) and FCF growth is also down (-1.4%), so the low valuation partly reflects a business that isn't expanding at the top line. The eye-catching 50.05% EPS growth likely reflects one-off or base-effect factors rather than durable operating momentum, given flat revenue — worth checking against reported results. Many balance-sheet and margin fields (gross margin, Debt/EBITDA, Altman Z, current ratio) are "n/a," typical for an insurer/asset manager, meaning some standard quality checks simply don't translate here. The net effect is a cheap, moderately stable financial whose weak growth and average quality temper the appeal of its valuation.

TROW.text:
T Rowe Price's #20 rank rests primarily on its Value and Quality scores. On valuation, a P/E of 12.13, P/B of 1.82, and P/FCF of 14.3 place it in the 73rd percentile — a reflection of the market pricing the asset manager conservatively. Quality (67.3) is backed by genuinely strong profitability: ROE of 19.48% and ROIC of 19.42% are healthy, operating margin sits at 30.73%, net margin at 28.28%, and the balance sheet carries zero debt with a current ratio of 3.64. The near-100% gross margin is characteristic of an asset manager, where fee revenue carries almost no cost of goods. Free cash flow growth of 17.2% and a 4.97% earnings surprise add support.

The drag comes from Momentum (26.7) and Growth (33.2). Revenue grew just 4.23% and EPS 5.66% year over year — modest for a business whose earnings are tethered to assets under management. The weak momentum score suggests the stock has lagged, which is worth pairing with the cheap valuation: a low P/E can signal value or can reflect investors' skepticism about future fee income.

Readers should double-check what the low multiple is discounting. Asset managers face structural pressure from fee compression and outflows toward passive products, so the modest revenue growth may not be a one-off. The zero-debt, high-margin profile is attractive, but sustainability of AUM-driven earnings — and whether the FCF growth is repeatable versus a favorable market year — deserves scrutiny before reading the value score as a bargain.

MU.text:
Micron's #5 ranking is powered almost entirely by its Momentum (100) and Growth (98.7) scores, both sitting at or near the top of the ranked universe. The growth figures are extraordinary: revenue up 167% year-over-year, EPS up roughly 700%, and free cash flow up over 1,278%, alongside a 17.3% earnings surprise. Quality is also strong at 74.7, supported by a 70.6% ROE, 61.5% ROIC, and margins that are exceptional for a hardware business — 72.6% gross, 65.6% operating, and 55.9% net. The balance sheet reinforces this: debt/equity of just 0.06, debt/EBITDA of 0.8, a current ratio of 3.42, an Altman Z-Score of 25, and a Piotroski F-Score of 8/9. Value is the clear laggard at 34.4, and a large insider-selling penalty (-15) is the single biggest drag on the final 60.8.

A reader should weigh a few things. Momentum pinned at exactly 100 means the stock is at the top of its run, so the score reflects how far it has already moved, not where it goes next. The growth rates are lapping unusually depressed prior-year comparisons — triple-digit expansion is unlikely to repeat, and future quarters will face far tougher year-over-year math. Valuation multiples (P/B 10.3, P/S 12.3, P/FCF 42) already embed rich expectations, explaining the weak Value score. Finally, the heavy insider selling against this backdrop is worth investigating directly, as it partly offsets the otherwise strong quality and growth signals.

HST.text:
Host Hotels & Resorts lands at #21 with a final score of 58.2, driven primarily by its Momentum (80.6) and Value (70.6) percentiles. On the value side, the numbers look reasonable for a REIT: a P/FCF of 10.62 and P/S of 2.62 suggest the stock isn't richly priced relative to cash generation, while the P/E of 20.96 and P/B of 2.44 are more middling. The strong momentum score indicates the shares have been performing well recently. Balance-sheet health is a standout — Debt/Equity of 0.19 and Debt/EBITDA of 0.77 are conservative for a property company, and the Piotroski F-Score of 8/9 signals broadly improving fundamentals. Growth is moderate (48.3), with revenue up 7.57% and EPS up 11.45% year-over-year, though FCF growth is essentially flat at 0.8%.

The weak link is Quality at 35.9. ROE of 11.67% and ROIC of 10.92% are only adequate, and net margin of 12.51% is thin enough that returns aren't distinguishing the business from peers. Several metrics are unavailable (gross margin, current ratio, Altman Z), typical for a REIT, so the model is working with a partial picture.

A reader should note the tension between high momentum and mediocre quality — an 80.6 momentum score late in a run can reverse quickly if hotel demand softens. The near-zero FCF growth also sits awkwardly against the healthier EPS figure, worth checking against occupancy trends, RevPAR, and how the low leverage might change if acquisitions ramp up.

INCY.text:
Incyte's #6 ranking (73.2/100) is powered primarily by an exceptional Growth score of 93.8, backed by 21.2% year-over-year revenue growth and outsized bottom-line acceleration — EPS up over 4,000% and FCF growth of 321%. Those triple-digit figures reflect earnings rebounding off a depressed prior-year base rather than sustainable run-rates, so they inflate the growth reading. Quality is also solid at 72.4: gross margin of nearly 93% is typical of a profitable biopharma, operating margin of 29.5% and ROE of 24.9% show real profitability, and the balance sheet looks pristine — a current ratio of 3.32, an Altman Z-Score of 10.48, and a Piotroski F-Score of 8/9 all point to financial strength with no visible leverage (debt figures are n/a). Momentum at 74.8 indicates the stock has participated in an upward move, while Value is middling at 56.1, with a P/E of 19.4, P/S of 4.86 and P/B of 4.83 — reasonable for the sector but not cheap.

Readers should be cautious about how much weight to place on the eye-catching growth rates; the astronomical EPS and FCF gains are base-effect distortions that will normalize and likely compress future growth scores. Biopharma revenue also hinges on concentration risk — a large share of Incyte's sales depends on a limited product portfolio and patent timelines worth verifying. With momentum already elevated, check whether the run has stretched the valuation, and confirm whether ROIC and debt data are simply unreported rather than genuinely absent.

FFIV.text:
F5's #24 ranking and 57.2 score are built mostly on the growth and momentum sides. Growth scores 69.2, supported by 9.66% year-over-year revenue growth, a stronger 23.88% EPS gain and 18.95% FCF growth — the earnings line is expanding faster than the top line, which points to improving profitability and operating leverage rather than just volume. Momentum at 62.8 says the stock has been outperforming much of the universe. Quality is respectable at 60.4, backed by a Piotroski F-Score of 8/9, high 81.41% gross margins, a 24.8% operating margin and 39.78% gross profit-to-assets, alongside a 19.28% ROE. The clear laggard is Value at 38.1: at a P/E of 31.7, P/S of 7.11 and P/B above 6, the market is already paying a premium for this quality and growth.

A few things worth checking. The value weakness is pulling directly against the other three factors, so the ranking hinges on growth and momentum continuing to justify that multiple — a P/E near 32 leaves little room for a growth stumble. With momentum elevated, it's worth asking how much of the recent run is already reflected in the price. Note the gaps in the data: ROIC, debt ratios and the Altman Z-Score are all listed as n/a, so leverage and true capital efficiency can't be verified here even though the current ratio of 1.56 looks adequate. The 23.88% EPS growth also outpaces revenue meaningfully — confirm whether that reflects durable margin gains or buyback-driven share-count reduction.

CINF.text:
Cincinnati Financial's #19 placement and 58.5 final score are anchored by a standout Value factor of 87.6. That reflects a P/E of just 11.17, a P/S of 2.12, and an attractive P/FCF of 8.64, suggesting the market is pricing the insurer cheaply relative to earnings and cash generation. The balance sheet reinforces the low-risk read: debt/equity of just 0.05 is negligible, and a 18.95% net margin alongside 15.04% ROE points to a profitable underwriting and investment operation. Growth is respectable at 59.8, helped by 11.41% revenue growth and a strong 17.7% jump in free cash flow, while Quality sits mid-pack at 53.6, consistent with a Piotroski score of 6/9 — solid but not pristine.

The clear drag is Momentum at 34.1, well below the other factors. That tells you the share price hasn't been rewarded lately despite the cheap valuation, so a reader should ask why the market is hesitant — value scores can persist for a long time if sentiment stays cool. Note too that EPS growth (4.61%) lags revenue growth (11.41%) meaningfully, which may hint at margin pressure, higher claims/catastrophe costs, or investment-income timing worth checking in the filings.

Several metrics are simply n/a because insurers don't report conventional gross/operating margins, ROIC, or Altman Z, so the Quality picture is partly incomplete. Given a P/B of 1.68 and book-value sensitivity typical of insurers, verify how reserves, catastrophe exposure, and investment-portfolio marks are trending before leaning on the headline value case.

NTAP.text:
NetApp lands at #11 with a 63.6 score driven overwhelmingly by Momentum (93.8) and solid Quality (74.4). The momentum reading tells you the stock has been one of the stronger performers in the universe, while the quality score is backed by genuinely impressive profitability: ROE of 94.5%, ROIC of 43.6%, gross margins of 67.5% and operating margins near 27%. A Piotroski F-Score of 7/9 and an Altman Z of 3.69 both point to a financially healthy, cash-generative business, and free-cash-flow growth of nearly 40% year-over-year is a real bright spot behind the numbers.

The offsetting weakness is Growth (36.8) and a middling Value score (41.9). Revenue actually declined 5.1% year-over-year, so the 10.3% EPS growth and strong FCF growth are being carried by margins, buybacks and cost discipline rather than a growing top line — worth checking how durable that is. On valuation, the P/E near 29 and P/S of 5.96 are not cheap, and the eye-catching 94% ROE is inflated by a very low equity base (P/B of 27.5 and Debt/Equity of 1.84), so the return figures flatter a leveraged balance sheet rather than signalling exceptional efficiency alone.

A reader should weigh the high momentum score carefully — it reflects a run that has already happened, not one that must continue — and confirm whether the shrinking revenue line is stabilizing. Leverage (Debt/EBITDA 1.34, current ratio 1.44) looks manageable but is the main reason the headline profitability ratios appear so extreme.

STT.text:
State Street's #3 ranking (73.9/100) is powered primarily by an exceptional Momentum score of 94.7 — the stock is running near the top of the ranked universe on price strength. Value backs this up at 79, supported by a modest P/E of 18.45, a P/B under 2.0, and a strikingly low P/FCF of 5.01, which suggests the market is pricing the company cheaply relative to the cash it throws off. Growth (63) and Quality (59.5) are respectable but more middling. The growth picture is uneven: revenue rose a steady 7.26% and EPS 14.74%, but the headline 176.7% FCF growth reflects a low or volatile prior-year base rather than a durable trend. Net margin of 21.12% is healthy for a custody/asset-servicing bank, though ROE of just 10.58% is unremarkable and explains the moderate Quality reading — this is a low-return, capital-heavy business.

Two things a reader should probe. First, a 94.7 momentum score this elevated often comes late in a run, meaning much of the good news may already be reflected in the $190.92 price; momentum can reverse quickly. Second, most balance-sheet and profitability diagnostics — ROIC, debt ratios, Altman Z, Piotroski F — are marked "n/a," which is common for financials but leaves leverage and asset quality largely unexamined here. The cheap P/FCF and strong FCF growth deserve a look at whether that cash flow is repeatable or a one-off. In short, momentum and value are doing the heavy lifting while quality quietly lags.

USB.text:
U.S. Bancorp lands at #27 with a final score of 57, and the ranking is carried primarily by Value (78.4). At a P/E of 12.84, P/B of 1.49 and P/FCF of 12.19, the stock screens cheaply against the broader universe, which is typical for large regional banks and consistent with a $97B market cap. Momentum is respectable at 63.5, and the Piotroski F-Score of 8/9 is a notable positive, signalling healthy fundamental trends across profitability, leverage and operating efficiency. Net margin of 26.42% and EPS growth of 20.41% year-over-year round out a picture of a bank whose earnings are improving off a low base.

The weaker inputs are Quality (46.2) and Growth (38.2). ROE of 11.61% is middling — solid but not exceptional for a bank — and revenue grew just 4.37%, so the strong EPS figure is being helped by factors other than top-line expansion (cost control, provisioning, or share dynamics). Readers should note that FCF fell 29.3%, which sits awkwardly against the flattering P/FCF and the high F-Score, so it is worth checking whether that decline is a one-off or a trend.

A few caveats: many bank-specific metrics (ROIC, margins, Altman Z, current ratio) are marked n/a, so the Quality read is incomplete. The low reported Debt/Equity of 0.26 also understates a bank's true leverage, since deposits and lending aren't captured the way they would be for an industrial. Interpret the "cheap" value score alongside interest-rate sensitivity and credit-cycle exposure.

MTB.text:
M&T Bank lands at #35 with a final score of 55.3, and its most influential driver is Value at 69.4. That reading is supported by a P/E of 13.39, a P/B of 1.31, and a P/FCF of 12.71 — modest multiples typical of a regional bank and cheaper than much of the broader market. The standout underlying signal is a perfect Piotroski F-Score of 9/9, which points to broad-based improvement in profitability, leverage, and operating efficiency and helps explain why Quality holds up at 53 despite a fairly ordinary ROE of 9.77%. EPS growth of 16.17% year-over-year outpaces revenue growth of 7.53%, suggesting margin or efficiency gains rather than pure top-line expansion. Momentum (51.5) and Growth (45.9) are middling, so this profile leans on being reasonably priced and fundamentally clean rather than fast-growing or trending.

A few figures warrant a closer look. Several bank-specific metrics — gross/operating margin, ROIC, current ratio, Altman Z — read "n/a," which is normal for financials but means the model is working with a thinner data set here. The reported net margin of 172% and P/S of 23 are artifacts of how bank revenue is measured and should not be taken at face value. FCF growth of -16.81% pulls against the otherwise improving picture and is worth reconciling against that 9/9 F-Score. Finally, ROE below 10% is unremarkable for the sector, so the Value score reflects a cheap stock more than an exceptional franchise — verify how rates and credit conditions are affecting earnings.

GOOGL.text:
Alphabet lands at #31 with a final score of 56.7, and its ranking is built on a fairly balanced spread across three of the four factors. Growth (72.3) is the standout, supported by 15.1% year-over-year revenue growth and a stronger 34.2% jump in EPS, suggesting operating leverage and margin discipline rather than growth bought at any cost. Momentum (68.9) and Quality (66.5) reinforce that picture: net margin of 32.8%, operating margin of 32.0%, ROE of 31.8% and ROIC of 27.7% describe a highly profitable business, while a debt/equity of just 0.12, a current ratio of 2.0 and an Altman Z-Score of 16.4 point to a fortress balance sheet with minimal solvency risk.

The clear drag is Value at 20.4 — a bottom-quintile score. At a P/E of 31.9, P/B of 10.2, P/S of 10.5 and a notably steep P/FCF of 57.6, the market is pricing in continued strong execution, so much of the quality and growth is already reflected in the price.

A few things worth checking behind the composite. The P/FCF gap versus the P/E hints at heavy capital spending, and indeed FCF growth was flat at just 0.69% despite 34% EPS growth — worth understanding whether that reflects AI/data-center investment or weakening cash conversion. The Piotroski score of 6/9 is solid but not pristine. Finally, elevated momentum this late in a large-cap run and a $4.2T market cap mean expectations are high, leaving less cushion if growth decelerates.

FDX.text:
FedEx lands at #18 largely on the strength of its Momentum (81.1) and Value (65.4) scores, which more than offset weaker Quality (31.9) and Growth (35.1). The momentum reading suggests the shares have been climbing relative to peers, while the value case rests on undemanding multiples: a P/E of 16.75, P/S of just 0.82, and P/FCF around 17. For a logistics business of this scale, that combination flags a stock the market is pricing conservatively even as recent earnings beat expectations by 4.78% and EPS grew 17.85% year-over-year.

The quality and growth picture is more sober. Operating margin of 6.2% and net margin of 4.88% are thin — the 62.6% gross margin doesn't survive the heavy cost of running a physical delivery network. ROIC of 8.88% is modest against a Debt/Equity of 0.85 and Debt/EBITDA of 2.1, and the Piotroski F-Score of 6/9 is middling. Revenue grew only 4.69%, so the strong EPS growth appears driven more by cost discipline and buybacks than by expansion.

A reader should weigh a few things. The high momentum score can arrive late in a run, so it's worth checking whether the recent move already reflects the earnings optimism. FCF actually shrank 4.9%, which sits awkwardly against the appealing P/FCF headline. PFS.text:

A reader should treat the eye-catching growth figures with caution. Note also that FCF growth was just 1.3%, a stark contrast to the headline EPS number. Finally, a sub-book valuation can signal either value or market skepticism about asset quality and net interest margin pressure.

SGHC.text:
SGHC lands at #22 with a 56.5 composite, and the profile is tilted toward Growth (71.6) and Quality (66.1) rather than Value. The Growth score is backed by real momentum in the underlying business: revenue grew nearly 20% year-over-year and EPS jumped 79.8%, suggesting operating leverage is flowing through as the top line scales. Quality is supported by an unusually strong return profile — ROE of 33.5% and ROIC of 30.1% — alongside a very light balance sheet, with Debt/Equity of just 0.14 and a current ratio of 1.61. A P/E of 30.75, P/B of 7.53 and P/S of 3.25 mean investors are already paying up for the growth and returns, which is why the Value factor drags against the other three. That premium leaves less room for error, and the latest earnings surprise came in at –3.88% — a modest miss worth watching against the priced-in expectations.

A few blanks deserve scrutiny: gross margin, Debt/EBITDA, Altman Z and Piotroski scores are all "n/a," so the quality read leans heavily on ROE and ROIC without the usual balance-sheet stress checks. Net margin of 10.58% is healthy but thinner than the operating margin of 16.81% suggests, hinting at meaningful below-the-line costs. Readers should confirm whether the triple-digit EPS growth is sustainable operating improvement or partly one-off effects.

SU.text:
Suncor's #34 rank and 53/100 score are propelled almost entirely by momentum (79.8), the standout factor here. That reflects strong recent price performance and a modest 4.68% earnings surprise. Value sits comfortably above average at 56.1, supported by an undemanding P/E of 15.64 and a P/FCF of 13.69 — reasonable multiples for a large integrated energy producer generating real cash. Quality is middling at 50.3: ROE of 14% and ROIC of 10.6% are respectable but not exceptional, while a low debt/equity ratio of 0.32 and a current ratio of 1.42 point to a conservatively financed balance sheet. The clear drag is Growth, scoring just 19.6. Revenue rose only 0.86% year-over-year, and although EPS grew 9%, the top line is essentially flat — a reminder that this is a mature, commodity-linked business whose fortunes track oil prices more than organic expansion.

A reader should be cautious about leaning on the momentum score: energy momentum is cyclical and can reverse quickly with crude prices, so a high reading late in a run warrants scrutiny of where oil sits. The "cheap" value signal may simply reflect the market pricing in that cyclicality. Note too that several diagnostics — Debt/EBITDA, Altman Z, Piotroski F-score — are unavailable, leaving gaps in the leverage and quality picture worth verifying independently.

M.text:
Macy's lands at #18 primarily on the strength of its Value factor, which sits at an exceptional 92.7. The valuation metrics justify this: a P/E of 9.04, P/B of just 1.04, P/S of 0.27, and a strikingly low P/FCF of 4.89. On price alone, the market is assigning very little premium to the business. Debt looks manageable (D/E 0.5, Debt/EBITDA 1.26, current ratio 1.48), but the modest Quality and Growth scores suggest the cheapness may be pricing in stagnation rather than a bargain.

OFG.text:

NTB.text:

Finally, Momentum being the weakest factor suggests price action lags the fundamentals — worth confirming whether that reflects sector-wide caution on banks rather than a company-specific issue.

INSW.text:
International Seaways tops the ranked universe largely on the strength of its Momentum score (96.6), which is by far its standout factor. That's reinforced by a striking 47.6% earnings surprise and 69.8% year-over-year EPS growth, signals that the tanker market has been running hot in its favor. Quality is also solid at 74.8, backed by genuinely impressive profitability: 27.1% ROE, 20.7% ROIC, and net margins above 55%. The balance sheet looks conservative too, with debt/equity of 0.27, debt/EBITDA of 1.16, a current ratio of 7.34, and an Altman Z-Score of 5.19 that suggests low bankruptcy risk. A Piotroski score of 7/9 rounds out a financially healthy picture. Value (55.6) and Growth (56.6) are middling — the 7.85 P/E looks cheap on the surface, but that's typical for cyclical shipping names.

The main thing to scrutinize is the cyclicality behind these numbers. Shipping companies post enormous margins and low P/Es at the top of freight-rate cycles, and a single-digit P/E often reflects the market pricing in an eventual downturn rather than a bargain. The 96.6 Momentum score, paired with a 47% earnings beat, may indicate this stock is late in a strong run rather than early. Note also that despite 14.5% revenue growth, free cash flow actually fell 11.8% year-over-year, and P/FCF of 31 is far less flattering than the trailing P/E. Worth checking whether current earnings and day rates are sustainable or peak-cycle figures.

ASB.text:
Associated Banc-Corp's #13 ranking and 61.5 composite are driven primarily by its Value and Growth factors, both sitting in the low-80s percentiles. On valuation, the stock trades at a P/E of 10.27, a P/S of 2.01, and notably a price-to-book of 0.86 — below the value of its net assets, which is common for regional banks the market views cautiously. The Growth score is inflated by eye-catching year-over-year figures: 90.85% revenue growth and 217.9% EPS growth, alongside a modest 1.88% earnings surprise. Quality is middling at 50.9, consistent with a 10.04% ROE, 8.5% ROIC, and healthy reported net (28.74%) and operating (35.92%) margins. The main thing to scrutinize is the growth data. Triple-digit EPS growth off a bank almost always reflects a depressed prior-year base — one-off charges, provisioning swings, or securities losses in the comparison period — rather than sustainable expansion; note FCF growth was only 6.1%, a far more sober number. The sub-1.0 P/B "cheapness" also deserves context: banks trade below book when investors doubt asset quality, deposit stability, or net-interest-margin durability, so a reader should check credit provisions, deposit trends and unrealized bond losses. Finally, the weak Momentum score (35.4) signals the market has not rewarded these results with price strength, pulling against the strong Value and Growth signals — worth reconciling before drawing conclusions.

AUB.text:

DHT.text:

A reader should verify where spot rates sit relative to history and how much of the momentum reflects a mature move rather than a fresh one.

MD.text:

THG.text:

Also worth noting: the Piotroski F-Score of 6/9 is decent but not exceptional, and net margin of 10.8% is thin in absolute terms, typical for a P&C insurer exposed to catastrophe volatility. The cheap valuation partly reflects that cyclicality — verify whether recent profitability is normal or peak.

EVR.text:

A reader should remember that advisory revenue is highly cyclical and lumpy — the 47% growth and 47% surprise are measured off a weak comparison period, so year-over-year figures may flatter the trend. The 99% "gross margin" is a services-accounting artifact; the more telling 22% operating and 16% net margins reflect heavy compensation costs. Missing Piotroski and Altman scores also leave some quality signals unverified.

BAP.text:

BOH.text:

WBS.text:

IFS.text:

MOG.B.text:

BNY.text:

The momentum reading reflects strong price performance that has pushed the stock to $162 and a $115B market cap. The growth score is backed by genuine improvement in the numbers: EPS grew 28.1% year-over-year against more modest 7.9% revenue growth, meaning most of the gains came from margin expansion and efficiency rather than the top line. Net margin of 27.6% and a Piotroski F-Score of 8/9 point to a financially healthy, well-run custody bank. Value (51.2) is middling — a P/E near 20.8 and P/B of 2.6 are reasonable but not cheap for a financial — and Quality (42.1) is the clear laggard, with ROE of just 12.5% sitting below what you'd want from a top-tier franchise.

A few things deserve a closer look. The eye-catching 762% FCF growth is almost certainly a low-base or timing artifact rather than a repeatable trend, so it should not be read as durable cash-flow acceleration. The high momentum score also raises the usual question of how much of the recent run is already priced in, especially with Value only average. The modest Quality score and sub-13% ROE pull against the stronger factors and suggest returns on capital are unremarkable for the sector. Debt/Equity of 0.72 is normal for a bank but, combined with many "n/a" balance-sheet metrics here, means leverage and asset quality warrant independent verification.

IVZ.text:
Invesco lands at #25 with a final score of 57.2, and that ranking is carried almost entirely by two factors: Value (81.7) and Momentum (84). The value case rests on a modest P/B of 1.2, a P/S of 2.3, and a reasonable P/FCF of about 10.2, which suggests the market is not paying a premium for the asset manager's cash generation. Momentum being in the 84th percentile indicates the share price has been on a strong run relative to peers. Growth is middling at 48.8, though the components are mixed — revenue grew 5.1% year-over-year and free cash flow jumped 28.6%, the latter being a genuine bright spot behind the value score.

The glaring weakness is Quality at 19.9, and the underlying metrics explain why. ROIC is negative at -4.95% and operating margin is -10.91%, while ROE and net margin read as n/a — signs of distorted or negative bottom-line profitability that the price-based value and momentum factors don't capture. Debt/Equity is low at 0.15, so leverage isn't the concern; earnings quality is.

A reader should double-check what's driving those negative returns and margins — asset managers can see reported profitability swung by intangibles, goodwill, or one-off items, so the FCF strength and the accounting losses tell conflicting stories. Also worth noting: an 84 momentum score can sit late in a run, meaning the strong Value/Momentum pairing is leaning on price behavior that a weak, unprofitable Quality profile is pulling against.

ACGL.text:
Arch Capital's #28 ranking and 56.9 overall score are carried almost entirely by an exceptional Value factor of 93.8. The valuation metrics back this up: a P/E of 8.47, P/B of 1.54, P/S of 1.87 and P/FCF of 6.08 are all cheap in absolute terms, particularly for an insurer generating an 18.17% ROE and a 22.07% net margin. Those profitability figures also lift Quality to a respectable 59.5, suggesting a business earning solid returns on its equity base. Growth sits mid-pack at 50.1, reflecting healthy 14.27% revenue growth that isn't yet flowing through to the bottom line.

The clear drag is Momentum at 22.2 — near the bottom of the universe. This tells you the market has not been rewarding the shares recently, which is often the flip side of a low valuation: cheap stocks are frequently cheap because sentiment or the earnings cycle has turned. That reading pairs with the growth internals, where EPS growth slowed to just 3.15% and free cash flow actually fell 7.46% year-over-year, despite double-digit revenue gains. In other words, the top line is expanding faster than earnings and cash are.

A reader should check why EPS and FCF are decelerating against rising revenue — for a P&C insurer this can reflect catastrophe losses, reserve development, or a softening pricing cycle. Note too that leverage, liquidity, and F-/Z-score data are unavailable here, so the Quality picture rests largely on ROE and margins rather than a full balance-sheet view.

ESS.text:
Essex Property Trust's #18 ranking and 59/100 final score are carried almost entirely by an exceptional Quality reading of 94.9 — a top-decile figure that reflects the durable, cash-generative nature of a West Coast apartment REIT. The standout metric is the 47.65% operating margin, which speaks to the pricing power and operational efficiency of owning irreplaceable coastal multifamily real estate. With no penalties applied and a P/FCF of 17.59, the business converts its rent roll into free cash flow reliably, which is what the model is rewarding here.

The other three factors are notably softer and pull the composite back toward the middle. Value sits at 48.1 — roughly average — with a P/B of 3.41 and P/S of 10.02 that are rich in absolute terms, though typical for a premium REIT. Momentum (42.8) and Growth (38.9) are both below the median: revenue grew just 6.36% year-over-year and FCF growth was essentially flat at 0.57%, so this is a slow-and-steady compounder rather than an accelerating story.

Readers should note how many fields read "n/a" — P/E, ROE, ROIC, Debt/EBITDA, and the Piotroski and Altman scores are all missing. REITs report FFO rather than standard net income, so conventional earnings and leverage metrics don't map cleanly, and the model may be leaning heavily on the few inputs it does have. Before drawing conclusions, verify the actual debt load and interest-rate sensitivity yourself, since balance-sheet leverage — a key REIT risk — isn't captured in these numbers.

BKNG.text:
Booking's #4 ranking and 73.6 score are carried almost entirely by two pillars: a perfect Value score of 100 and a strong Quality score of 86.6. On the quality side the standout is a 58.68% ROIC alongside a 32.79% operating margin, evidence of an asset-light, highly profitable platform business that converts revenue efficiently into returns. An Altman Z-Score of 4.21 signals low bankruptcy risk and Debt/EBITDA of 2.18 is manageable. Growth is respectable but not spectacular at 71.1, backed by 13.39% year-over-year revenue growth and 15.11% FCF growth. The clear laggard is Momentum at 33.6, meaning the shares have underperformed peers on a trailing basis even as the fundamentals rank near the top.

The most important thing to double-check here is the Value data itself. A P/S of 0.26 and P/FCF of 0.76 are wildly out of line with a company earning 58% ROIC — these figures, together with a $213 price and a $7B market cap that don't match BKNG's actual scale, suggest a data error or split/share-count issue feeding the perfect Value score. Treat that 100 skeptically until verified against reported financials. Note too the many "n/a" fields (P/E, P/B, ROE, net margin, Piotroski), which limit how completely the model can assess the business. Finally, the weak momentum pulling against strong quality and growth is worth understanding: it may reflect a genuine sentiment gap, or simply a stock the market has left behind for reasons the trailing fundamentals don't yet capture.

KEY.text:
KeyCorp's #14 ranking and 61.5 final score are propelled almost entirely by Growth (94.9) and Value (79.9). The growth figure reflects some striking year-over-year moves — 62.7% revenue growth and 250.8% FCF growth — while the value case rests on a modest P/E of 13.1, a P/B of 1.18 that sits close to book value, and a P/FCF near 11.4. A Piotroski F-Score of 8/9 is a strong signal of improving financial health, and a 24.3% net margin plus manageable Debt/Equity of 0.49 round out a picture of a bank whose fundamentals appear to be recovering.

That said, Quality (40.5) and Momentum (41.5) are both middling and act as a drag. The clue is in ROE of just 8.97% — well below what investors typically expect from a healthy bank — which suggests profitability is still subdued despite the headline growth. This is where readers should be careful: the enormous revenue and FCF growth rates almost certainly reflect a recovery off a depressed prior-year base rather than sustainable expansion, so they may not repeat. The strong value multiples could equally signal that the market remains skeptical about earnings durability.

Because banking metrics like gross margin, operating margin, ROIC and Altman Z are marked n/a, this model can't fully assess asset quality or interest-rate sensitivity. Worth double-checking independently: net interest margin trends, deposit stability, credit-loss provisions, and whether that low-single-digit ROE is improving or stuck.

RL.text:
Ralph Lauren's #30 placement (final score 56.8) is powered chiefly by Growth (74.9) and solid Quality (60.8). The growth picture is genuinely broad: revenue up 14.6% year-over-year, EPS up 30%, and free cash flow up 13.3%, suggesting expansion that is flowing through to the bottom line rather than just the top. Quality metrics reinforce this — ROE of 33.1% and ROIC of 28.9% are strong for a consumer brand, a 69.9% gross margin reflects real pricing power, and a perfect Piotroski F-Score of 9/9 alongside an Altman Z-Score of 6.14 points to clean, healthy financials. The balance sheet is conservative, with Debt/Equity of 0.44, Debt/EBITDA under 1.0, and a current ratio of 2.13.

Value is middling at 53: a P/E of 24 and P/S of 2.79 are not cheap, and the P/B of 7.96 is elevated, though ROE that high partly justifies a rich book multiple. The clear drag is Momentum at 41.2, sitting well below the other factors and pulling against an otherwise strong profile — worth checking whether the market has cooled on the shares even as fundamentals improved.

Readers should note the gap between operating margin (14.5%) and that headline 69.9% gross margin, indicating heavy SG&A and marketing spend typical of a luxury apparel house. Growth this strong also invites scrutiny of sustainability — apparel demand is cyclical and discretionary, so verify whether the 30% EPS jump reflects durable trends or a favorable comparison period.

PAYX.text:
Paychex lands at #34 with a 56/100 final score, and the ranking is powered primarily by Quality (69.5) and Growth (67.6). The quality profile is genuinely strong: ROE of 47.1% and ROIC of 30.3% point to a highly capital-efficient business, while margins are the kind you'd expect from an entrenched payroll and HR services operator — 74.3% gross, 38.6% operating, and 27% net. The Piotroski F-Score of 8/9 and an Altman Z of 3.38 both reinforce operational and balance-sheet health. On the growth side, revenue rose 16.9% year-over-year and free cash flow jumped 35.9%, which is what lifts the growth percentile.

The weaker factors are Value (46.8) and Momentum (39.8), and they explain why the overall score sits in the mid-50s rather than higher. Investors are paying up for this quality: a P/E of 25.7, P/S of 6.9, and an eye-catching P/B of 12.1 all signal a premium valuation, so the "value" here is middling at best. The soft momentum score suggests the stock hasn't been a recent market leader.

A few things worth double-checking. EPS growth of just 6.6% lags the 16.9% revenue growth — a gap that may reflect acquisition-related dilution or cost pressure, so verify how much of that top-line jump is organic. Debt/Equity of 1.22 looks elevated, though Debt/EBITDA of 1.54 is modest and partly reflects the low equity base behind that high P/B. The premium multiple leaves little margin for a growth disappointment.

MNST.text:
Monster Beverage lands at #15 with a final score of 61.4, and the ranking is carried by three broadly balanced factors: Momentum and Growth both at 69.5, and Quality at 68. The Quality reading is well supported by the underlying business economics — a 55.85% gross margin, a 29.17% operating margin, and gross profit equal to 46.37% of assets all point to a highly profitable, asset-light consumer franchise. The current ratio of 3.7 signals a very comfortable liquidity position. Growth is respectable rather than explosive: revenue rose 10.7% year-over-year and free cash flow grew 18.11%, consistent with a mature but still-expanding beverage maker. The clear laggard is Value at 38.8, which drags on the composite.

That weak Value score is worth understanding before reading too much into the rest. The stock trades at 5.78x book, 5.76x sales, and roughly 24x free cash flow — investors are paying a premium for the quality and growth, so much of the good news may already be reflected in the price. A Momentum score near 70 also invites a check on where the stock sits in its run, since late-stage momentum can reverse.

Finally, note how many fields are marked "n/a" — P/E, ROE, ROIC, net margin, debt ratios, and the Piotroski and Altman scores are all missing. That means the Quality figure rests on margins alone, without confirmation from returns on capital or leverage data, so a reader should verify profitability and balance-sheet strength directly.

HG.text:
Hamilton Insurance Group tops the ranking on a broad-based profile rather than one dominant factor. Value is the strongest leg at 92.3, built on a 1.25 price-to-book, 1.21 price-to-sales and a 4.18 price-to-free-cash-flow — the last of which is unusually low even for a specialty insurer. Growth (73.8) reflects 36% year-over-year revenue growth, consistent with a company writing considerably more premium, while free cash flow grew a more modest 11%. Quality scores 83.1 largely on balance-sheet conservatism: debt-to-equity of 0.05 is minimal, and momentum at 80.9 indicates the shares have participated in the recent re-rating of the sector.

The caveat is how much of the underlying data is unavailable. There is no P/E, no ROE or ROIC, no margin data, no Piotroski or Altman score — so the Quality reading is resting on leverage and a narrow set of inputs rather than demonstrated returns on capital. For an insurer, the metrics that actually matter are the combined ratio, prior-year reserve development, and growth in book value per share; none of those feed this model. A 4x price-to-free-cash-flow figure at an insurer often reflects premium float inflows, which are liabilities in waiting, not owner earnings.

Two things worth checking independently: whether that 36% revenue growth came from favorable pricing or from expanding into riskier lines late in a hardening market, and how much of book value is sensitive to bond mark-to-market. Momentum this strong after a sector-wide run also raises the question of what is already priced in.

I'll research Hamilton Insurance Group's current situation.THESIS: Hamilton compounds book value by pairing an underwriting book increasingly weighted to US E&S and casualty/specialty with an unusual investment structure. Q2 2026 produced net income of $144 million, a 21% annualized return on average equity and a 95% combined ratio that absorbed roughly $50 million of catastrophe losses, with gross premiums written up 17%. Book value per share reached $28.91 with accumulated dividends of $2.00, taking the combined metric to $30.91 versus $17.35 at IPO — 78% growth since listing. The mechanism is mid-teens premium growth at a low-to-mid-90s combined ratio, plus an investment return most peers cannot replicate, retained and partly recycled through buybacks.

WHAT MUST GO RIGHT: E&S and casualty rate adequacy must persist while Hamilton grows into it; management reaffirmed low double-digit growth and a low-to-mid-90s combined ratio, which requires reserve additions to stay absent. The Two Sigma engine must keep delivering — the fund returned 5.1% net in Q2 with investment income of $141 million — and the new governance must not impair liquidity. The AM Best upgrade of Hamilton Select to A must convert into wholesale broker shelf space rather than just optionality.

WHAT COULD BREAK THE THESIS: adverse development on the 2022–2025 casualty years; a Two Sigma drawdown quarter that turns book value negative, as already happened once — BVPS fell 3.8% in Q1 2026 to $27.42; a soft-market year where GPW growth continues while margins do not; or a repeat of concentrated event losses like the $46 million Middle East conflict charge and 2025's $142.8 million California wildfire loss.

GROWTH DRIVERS: organic, not acquisitive. FY2025 gross premiums written rose 20.7% to $2.9 billion with net premiums earned up 21.6%, and Q2 growth came from casualty and specialty classes. New units are being built, not bought: Mike Mulray was promoted to President of Hamilton Select effective July 1, 2026 as the company scales its wholesale-only distribution, and a Private Clients business launched within Hamilton Global Specialty under Jamie Keaney effective June 1, 2026. Per-share growth is aided by buybacks: 7,102,791 shares repurchased for $163.3 million under the 2024 program.

MOAT: modest but strengthening at the edges. The durable advantages are Lloyd's, Bermuda, Ireland and US licences, and the Two Sigma relationship. The Select upgrade to A expands access to US specialty business. Against that, specialty underwriting is replicable capital; management itself describes a market that remains competitive amid social and economic inflation. Call it stable-to-strengthening in distribution, stable in underwriting.

VALUATION: the stock traded at $36.01 near a 52-week high of $37.31, against $2.9 billion of shareholders' equity and $6.1 billion of cash and invested assets — roughly 1.25x the reported $28.91 book value. That embeds continuation of high-teens-plus returns on equity, not a discount. The market is paying up for the compounding, so disappointment is priced asymmetrically.

CATALYSTS: Q3 2026 results (early November, date not yet confirmed); North Atlantic hurricane season through November; January 1 reinsurance renewals as the pricing tell; further buyback activity following program completion; any new special dividend, after the 2025 special dividend paid March 30, 2026.

RISKS: the bear case is that Hamilton is a levered bet on two volatile inputs. Q2's 95% combined ratio missed the 89.2% consensus by 580 basis points and net income fell from $187 million a year earlier — the EPS beat came substantially from investments, not underwriting. The April 1, 2026 Investment Agreement requires Hamilton Re to maintain the lesser of $1.8 billion or 60% of net tangible assets in the fund, with a two-tier withdrawal structure and liquidity limits, formalising concentration and constraining exit. Growing casualty premium 17% into a competitive market is precisely how reserve problems are made.

DATA CONFIDENCE: VERIFIED — Q2 and FY2025 results, BVPS series, buyback totals, Select's AM Best upgrade, the Two Sigma agreement terms, Mulray and Keaney appointments, the $36.01 price. INTERPRETATION — moat direction, the read that investment income carried the quarter, and the implied ~1.25x book. FORECAST — none offered. NOT VERIFIED — insider transactions, institutional ownership changes, analyst estimate revisions after Q2, exact Q3 report date, current reserve development detail, and the end-year of the CEO contract extension.

THESIS MONITOR: WHAT CHANGED — little in direction, more in texture. Book value per share and the Two Sigma contribution are unchanged from the previous note, confirming that thesis was current. New since: the Select upgrade to A, the completed $163.3 million buyback, the Private Clients launch, and reaffirmed guidance. Negative: the combined-ratio miss and lower year-on-year net income. Governance: the CEO's employment agreement was amended to extend her term — continuity, not a change. WHY IT MATTERS — the mix-shift leg of the thesis got harder evidence via the rating upgrade and Select leadership build; the margin leg got weaker evidence. WHETHER TEMPORARY OR STRUCTURAL — the cat losses are event-driven and temporary; the formalised Two Sigma minimum commitment is structural and makes the balance sheet permanently less conventional. WHETHER STILL VALID — yes; the four legs described previously are intact, with the caveat that the price now sits near its high rather than at a discount.

VERDICT: unchanged
